title_en: MacroVoices #550 Harley Bassman: In FED We Trust
title_zh: MacroVoices #550 Harley Bassman：In FED We Trust（我们信任美联储）
subtitle_zh: Convexity Maven Harley Bassman 谈美联储重建市场信任、财政赤字与抵押债券凸性风险。
description: MacroVoices #550 Harley Bassman: In FED We Trust

turns.en: What's going on, in my view, is we have a lack of trust in the government, in a lot of our institutions, and maybe about the Fed. What's really important here is the Fed needs to go and regain the trust of the market.
turns.zh: 在我看来，现在的情况是，大家对政府、对很多机构、乃至对美联储都缺乏信任。这里真正重要的是，美联储需要去重新赢得市场的信任。

turns.en: That was Harley Bassman, the fixed income guru who invented the Move Index, and who's best known on the street as the Convexity Maven. I'm Eric Townsend, and this is Macrovoices, the free weekly podcast targeting professional finance and sophisticated private investors.
turns.zh: 刚才那位是 Harley Bassman，固定收益界的泰斗，MOVE 指数（Move Index）的发明人，在华尔街以“凸性专家”（Convexity Maven）著称。我是 Eric Townsend，这里是 MacroVoices，一档面向专业金融人士和成熟个人投资者的免费周播节目。

turns.en: Episode 550 was produced September 17th, 2026. Just hours before this week's feature interview was recorded, the Federal Reserve surprised hawkishly by not just hiking rates like everyone knew they were going to, but also signaling that another rate hike is likely to occur before Christmas.
turns.zh: 第 550 期制作于 2026 年 9 月 17 日。就在本周主访谈录制前几个小时，美联储给了市场一个鹰派的意外——不仅像大家预料的那样加了息，还暗示圣诞节前很可能再加一次。

turns.en: So Harley and I will start with the news and what it means, then move into a slide deck Harley prepared, giving us his tech on markets and where they're headed.
turns.zh: 所以 Harley 和我会先聊聊这条新闻以及它的含义，然后进入 Harley 准备的一份幻灯片，听听他对市场以及后市走向的看法。

turns.en: You'll find the slide deck linked in your research roundup email or at macrovoices.com. And I'm Patrick Ceresna. Let's dive straight into this interview.
turns.zh: 你可以在 research roundup 邮件里找到这份幻灯片的链接，或者上 macrovoices.com。我是 Patrick Ceresna。我们直接进入本期访谈。

turns.en: Harley, I'm going to have to hit you up here. Sorry to do this to you, but you sent us a slide deck a couple of days ago, and the title of it is In Fed We Trust.
turns.zh: Harley，我得拿这个问问你。抱歉这么对你，但你几天前发给我们一份幻灯片，标题是 In Fed We Trust（我们信任美联储）。

turns.en: Now we're recording this on Wednesday afternoon after the hawkish surprise. We had an expected rate hike, but then it went unexpectedly hawkish with a dot plot saying that's not the last hike in 2026.
turns.zh: 我们是在这个鹰派意外之后的周三下午录的这期。加息本来在预期之内，但结果意外地偏鹰，点阵图（dot plot）显示这还不是 2026 年的最后一次加息。

turns.en: And that really shocked markets. So do you still trust the Fed this afternoon, Harley? Thank you for having me back on. I appreciate it. You have the best financial podcast on the planet, and it's an honor to be here.
turns.zh: 这确实震惊了市场。那么今天下午你还信任美联储吗，Harley？——谢谢你们再次邀请我，我很感激。你们做的是地球上最好的金融播客，能来这里是我的荣幸。

turns.en: My last two commentaries have been advocating strongly for the Fed to hike 50. What and done, get it done. What's going on here? I think people are a little confused, actually, they're not confused at all.
turns.zh: 我最近两篇评论一直在强烈主张美联储加息 50 个基点，一步到位、干脆利落。现在到底是什么情况？我觉得大家有点困惑——其实，他们一点也不困惑。

turns.en: We know that the economy or inflation, it's not going to matter if they go 25, 50, or even 100 for God's sakes. I mean, that really is not going to change a whole lot right now.
turns.zh: 我们知道，对经济或通胀来说，加 25、50、甚至老天爷啊加 100 个基点，其实都无所谓。我的意思是，眼下这真的不会改变太多东西。

turns.en: What's going on in my view is we have a lack of trust in the government, in a lot of our institutions, and maybe about the Fed. And I think what's really important here is the Fed needs to go and regain the trust of the market.
turns.zh: 在我看来，现在的情况是，大家对政府、对很多机构、乃至对美联储都缺乏信任。我觉得这里真正重要的是，美联储需要去重新赢得市场的信任。

turns.en: There's an adult in the room, this hand on the steering wheel that's going to kind of guide the world's largest economy or not economy currency.
turns.zh: 要让屋里有个靠谱的成年人，有一只手握着方向盘，去引导全球最大的经济体——或者说全球最大的货币。

turns.en: And that's where it's at. And I think what he's trying to do is slowly get us off of forward guidance and other dot plots. Get off of that and get us back to the good old days where the market actually assessed risk and managed its risk accordingly, as opposed to being dependent upon the Fed and everything else.
turns.zh: 关键就在这里。我觉得他想做的，是慢慢让我们戒掉前瞻指引（forward guidance）和那些点阵图，摆脱这些东西，回到过去的好时光——那时候市场真正自己去评估风险、相应地管理风险，而不是依赖美联储和其他一切。

turns.en: And I think what you've seen in the past is that markets have gotten over their skis when the Fed gives too much guidance that changes their mind.
turns.zh: 我想你过去见过的是，当美联储给出太多指引、然后又改主意时，市场就会冲得太猛、失去平衡。

turns.en: I think what's happening right now is getting off forward guidance is like coming off smoking or I'd say heroin actually, but there's a family broadcast here.
turns.zh: 我觉得现在正在发生的是，戒掉前瞻指引就像戒烟——其实我更想说像戒海洛因，但这是档合家欢节目，就这么一说。

turns.en: It's just hard to get off of it. And the market is becoming more volatile as we slowly back away. And I kind of think right now, cold turkey would have been the better idea.
turns.zh: 它就是很难戒。而随着我们慢慢后撤，市场正变得越来越波动。我甚至觉得，眼下一次性硬戒反而是更好的主意。

turns.en: Up 50 would have been fine. The market was already priced for it. What are you waiting for? You've got tortures for another 12 weeks because they're not going in October, clearly, before the election.
turns.zh: 加 50 个基点本来完全没问题。市场早就已经把这个价格计入了。你们还在等什么？现在好了，还得再被折磨 12 周，因为他们显然不会在 10 月、在大选前动手。

turns.en: So we're going to wait 12 weeks to go and do 25 more and then think about it. So this was not a good result today. It should have been zero or 50, in my view.
turns.zh: 所以我们要等上 12 周，再加 25 个基点，然后再琢磨下一步。所以今天这不是个好结果。在我看来，本该是 0 或者 50。

turns.en: Okay. Let's talk about what comes next now because as you just said, you're describing a Federal Reserve that's kind of taken the steering wheel wanting to show the market.
turns.zh: 好。那我们来聊聊接下来会发生什么，因为正如你刚说的，你描述的是一个已经握住方向盘、想给市场看点颜色的美联储。

turns.en: There's an adult at the wheel where your words, okay, you know, something else we saw in very recent history was some people in the AI community spoke up and called for a slowdown in the progress of their own organization.
turns.zh: 用你的话说，方向盘后面坐着个成年人。好，你知道，我们最近在历史上还看到另一件事：AI 圈里有一些人站出来，呼吁放慢他们自己所在领域的进展。

turns.en: It resulted in a pretty darn emotional reaction from some senior officials in the U.S. government, including the very top. And I'm not sure if we're necessarily feeling in that debate like it's the adults that are feuding with one another.
turns.zh: 结果引来了美国政府一些高级官员——包括最高层——相当情绪化的反应。我不确定在那场争论里，我们能不能感觉到是“成年人”在互相掐架。

turns.en: Is there a risk that the Fed is about to get into a fight with the Trump administration? And if so, how do you see that playing out? Geez, you know, Mom always said, don't discuss politics or religion in polite company.
turns.zh: 美联储有没有可能马上就要和 Trump 政府干起来？如果有，你觉得会怎么演？——天，你知道，妈妈总说，在讲究的场合别谈政治或宗教。

turns.en: So I'm kind of like nervous about going where you're kind of taking me into because that is where the lack of trust, it's not good guy, bad guy.
turns.zh: 所以你把我往这个方向带，我还有点紧张，因为那正是“缺乏信任”的地方，它不是好人对坏人那么简单。

turns.en: It's if you say something, do you follow through that sort of trust? And we know that the Fed is a special entity. The Supreme Court, a few weeks ago, ruled that basically the executive branch, the president can basically do what he wants to do.
turns.zh: 而是——你说了话，会不会兑现，这才是那种信任。我们知道美联储是个特殊的实体。几周前最高法院裁定，基本上行政部门、总统想干什么就能干什么。

turns.en: We could fire or hire anybody at will. They carved out the Fed. Now, the Fed really is an arm of the government. So logically, I guess if you could deal with the FCC or something else that, well, why not be able to deal with the Fed?
turns.zh: 他可以随意解雇或雇用任何人。但他们把美联储单独划了出来。要知道，美联储其实是政府的一条胳膊。所以按理说，我猜如果你能处置 FCC 或其他机构，那为什么不能处置美联储呢？

turns.en: They said, no, the Fed is too special. It's too important. Basically, as the governor on the World Reserve currency and the president can't touch, the executive branch can't touch them.
turns.zh: 他们说，不行，美联储太特殊、太重要了。基本上，作为世界储备货币的掌舵者，总统碰不得，行政部门也碰不得。

turns.en: And I think that underlines the idea of the importance of gaining credibility and trust in the Fed, notwithstanding a lack of trust in other parts of the government.
turns.zh: 我觉得这恰恰凸显了一点：即便对政府其他部分缺乏信任，在美联储身上建立公信力和信任依然至关重要。

turns.en: Harley, we talked about the presidential administration overall, but let's narrow it a little bit more to specifically the Treasury Department.
turns.zh: Harley，我们谈了总统政府这个整体，但我们再缩小一点，专门聊聊财政部（Treasury Department）。

turns.en: What do you think? If the Fed and Treasury get along, does that solve everything or do we need the Fed and the entire administration to agree on rates?
turns.zh: 你怎么看？如果美联储和财政部合得来，是不是就万事大吉了？还是说我们需要美联储和整个政府在利率问题上达成一致？

turns.en: Where does this go? And more importantly, do you see a secretary Besant and the Fed, FOMC, you know, do you think they're going to get along?
turns.zh: 这会走向何方？更重要的是，你觉得 Besant 财长和美联储、FOMC，他们能合得来吗？

turns.en: Look, clearly, we have various activities going on between the executive branch, the congressional branch, and between various political parties, which are bothersome for everybody.
turns.zh: 听着，显然，行政部门、国会部门以及各党派之间有各种角力，这些对每个人来说都很烦人。

turns.en: I think that if the Fed or and Treasury, Besant, if they can, I don't want to say hold hands, but if they can go and work in a symbiotic manner, not a 1951 Fed accord, you know, in public, but if they can work in a symbiotic manner, I think that's good enough.
turns.zh: 我觉得，如果美联储和财政部、和 Besant，如果他们能——我不想说手拉手——但如果他们能以共生的方式合作，不是像 1951 年《美联储-财政部协议》（1951 Fed accord）那样公开签个约，而是私下以共生方式协作，我觉得那就够好了。

turns.en: If the people think, if investors think, if foreign governments think that the financial policy of the United States, printer of the world's reserve currency, is the adult in the room managing things with squabbles everywhere else, but the two dead mom or dad and dad, in this case, I suppose, they're in a coordinated fashion where they got things under control and there's a path to a good result.
turns.zh: 如果民众、如果投资者、如果外国政府都认为，作为世界储备货币印刷者的美国，其金融政策是屋里那个管事的大人，别处吵吵闹闹，但这两位——本该是妈和爸，但这个情形下我猜是爸和爸——他们以协调一致的方式把事情控制住，并且有一条通向好结果的路径。

turns.en: That doesn't mean a good result today. A path to a good result. I think that's good enough. And I think that's happening right now. And Warsh is just having a, he's going slowly.
turns.zh: 这不意味着今天就有好结果，而是有一条通向好结果的路径。我觉得这就够好了。而且我认为这正在发生。Warsh 只是在——他在慢慢来。

turns.en: And I think, you know, to get his 12-0 vote today, he had to basically, you know, swallow hard and do 25. He probably wanted to do 50, I suppose, or he should have wanted to do 50 and get done with, but having unanimity was a good result.
turns.zh: 我觉得，为了今天拿到 12 比 0 的投票，他基本上得咬牙加 25 个基点。他大概本想加 50，或者说他本该想加 50、一步了结，但能全票通过是个好结果。

turns.en: And so, yeah, it's going to hurt, you know, until December. But yeah, we're going there, I think. I think we're going there. Listeners, Harley prepared a slide deck to accompany this week's interview.
turns.zh: 所以，是的，这会有点难受，一直熬到 12 月。但是的，我觉得我们正在往那个方向走。各位听众，Harley 为本周的访谈准备了一份幻灯片。

turns.en: You'll definitely want to download that. You can find it linked in your research roundup email. We've also tried to make this a little easier for you.
turns.zh: 你一定会想下载它。你可以在 research roundup 邮件里找到链接。我们也尽量把这件事变得对你更方便一些。

turns.en: It's no longer necessary to pass a registration wall. If you just want to download, click the button above Harley's picture on our homepage, macrovoices.com says looking for the downloads.
turns.zh: 现在不必再翻过注册墙了。如果你只想下载，点我们主页 macrovoices.com 上 Harley 头像上方的按钮，那里写着“寻找下载”。

turns.en: That's been reprogrammed, hopefully it's working now, to take you to a page where you can download directly or you can subscribe to the research roundup email or both, whatever suits your fancy.
turns.zh: 那个按钮已经重新编程了，希望现在能用了，它会把你带到一个页面，你可以直接下载，或者订阅 research roundup 邮件，或者两样都来，随你喜欢。

turns.en: Harley, let's dive into the slide deck. Which page number do you want to start on? Page four is fine. Let's dial back here. I'm really not going to talk about numbers.
turns.zh: Harley，我们进入这份幻灯片吧。你想从第几页开始？——第 4 页就行。我们往回说一点。我其实不打算谈数字。

turns.en: Do I think I can make an economic case for the fed to hike rates? No, I don't. As a matter of fact, I can do a lot of cases that they could have held rates flat.
turns.zh: 我觉不觉得我能从经济学角度论证美联储该加息？不，我不觉得。事实上，我能给出很多理由说明他们本可以按兵不动、维持利率不变。

turns.en: But that's not the deal here. It's a matter of building trust and trust has been damaged. And why has it been damaged? Slide four, corporate profits as a part of GDP basically doubled.
turns.zh: 但问题不在这里。这是建立信任的问题，而信任已经受损了。为什么受损？看第 4 页，企业利润占 GDP 的比重基本上翻了一倍。

turns.en: Going from 6% to 12%. We can, you know, wave our hands about why it's happened. Has it been because of the big tech firms? Is it because of government policy or who knows what?
turns.zh: 从 6% 涨到了 12%。我们可以比比划划地猜为什么会出现这种情况。是因为大型科技公司吗？是因为政府政策吗？还是别的什么原因，谁知道呢？

turns.en: But clearly this feeling is going through the economy and people are basically being unhappy about it. The next S&P versus Michigan sentiment.
turns.zh: 但显然，这种情绪正弥漫在整个经济体中，人们基本上对此感到不满。下一张，标普（S&P）对比密歇根（Michigan）消费者信心指数。

turns.en: This is a really hard slide to read. I'll just sum it up that in general, what we had was these two things went in line when people felt better, stocks went higher when they felt worse, stocks went the other way.
turns.zh: 这张幻灯片很难读懂。我就总结一下：大体上，这两条线原本是同步的——人们感觉好些时，股市就涨；感觉差些时，股市就往反方向走。

turns.en: And what you've seen in the last X number of months is this alligator jaw opening of stocks going up and sentiment going down, which is basically just a measure of this distrust.
turns.zh: 而在过去若干个月里，你看到的是像鳄鱼嘴一样张开的口子：股市往上、信心往下，这基本上就是对那种不信任的一种度量。

turns.en: Next, housing affordability. It's terrible. It's as bad as it's been in 30 years. And affordability is simply, you know, median income versus median house price versus the interest rate.
turns.zh: 接下来，住房可负担性。糟糕透顶，是 30 年来最差的水平。而可负担性说白了，就是中位数收入对比中位数房价再对比利率。

turns.en: And basically if house prices go up, incomes not rise that much and rates go up and nobody is happy when they can't buy a house. It should be 61, 2, 3, 4% of the population and people and it's well known that the best family results occur in an intact family in a house.
turns.zh: 基本上，如果房价上涨、收入却没涨那么多、利率又往上走，那么当人们买不起房时，没人会开心。这本该覆盖人口中相当大的比例，而且大家也都知道，最好的家庭结果，往往出现在一个完整家庭住在一套房子里的时候。

turns.en: They all kind of all go together and that's not happening right now. Where you really see the break apart is the next slide in the age of the first home being bought.
turns.zh: 这些东西都是相辅相成的，而现在这种情况并没有发生。你真正能看到断裂的地方，是下一张幻灯片——首次购房的年龄。

turns.en: It's basically gone from 32, 33 age to 38 in like five, six years. This is terrible. Now, is it a public policy result? Is it more random? Hard to say, but it's a reality that's happened and no one can be happy with this kind of result.
turns.zh: 它基本上在五六年的时间里，从 32、33 岁涨到了 38 岁。这太糟糕了。那么，这是公共政策的结果吗？还是更偏向偶然？很难说，但这是已经发生的现实，没人会对这样的结果感到高兴。

turns.en: Harley, let's continue the slide deck on page eight, bank versus non-bank landing. So this is not news over here. We all know that the big non-bankers are coming in, private credit.
turns.zh: Harley，我们接着看幻灯片第 8 页，银行放贷对比非银行放贷。——这块其实不算新闻。我们都知道大型非银行机构正在进场，也就是私募信贷（private credit）。

turns.en: Is that going to be a problem someday? Yeah, probably, but it doesn't matter. What's happening here is the non-bank entities are disintermediating the banking system.
turns.zh: 这将来会不会成为问题？会，很可能会，但这不重要。这里正在发生的是，非银行实体正在对银行体系进行“去中介化”（disintermediating）。

turns.en: This is important because it just reduces the ability of the Fed to transmit their policy to the overall economy because banks basically work with the Fed.
turns.zh: 这之所以重要，是因为它削弱了美联储把政策传导到整个经济体的能力，因为银行基本上是跟着美联储走的。

turns.en: They borrow from the Fed. They price off the Fed. These non-bank entities, they're a little lower down in the capital structure and they lend as they want to.
turns.zh: 银行向美联储借钱，按美联储的利率定价。而这些非银行实体，它们在资本结构（capital structure）里位置更靠下，想怎么放贷就怎么放贷。

turns.en: They're not as impacted by the Fed's rate. So once again, trust becomes more important than the policy rate itself. Slide nine, I think this is where the rubber meets the road about why rates are going up so much over here, aside from the lack of trust, is that there's just massive price insensitive demand.
turns.zh: 他们受美联储利率的影响没那么大。所以再一次，信任变得比政策利率本身更重要。第 9 页，我觉得这里才是见真章的地方——除了缺乏信任之外，利率之所以在这边涨这么多，是因为存在巨量的、对价格不敏感的需求。

turns.en: The hyperscalers here on page nine, this is a projection. Is it going to happen? Who knows? But I mean, these numbers are out of control. You're talking about 750 million projected borrowing.
turns.zh: 第 9 页上这些超大规模云厂商（hyperscalers），这是一个预测。它会不会成真？谁知道呢？但我是说，这些数字已经失控了。你说的是预计 7.5 亿的借款。

turns.en: The Treasury has issued $2 billion. We're getting close to a 30-35% competition for money. The Fed can't stop this. There's nothing they could do, per se, because these guys are going to borrow money at any rate, six, eight, 10, 12.
turns.zh: 财政部已经发行了 20 亿美元。我们正接近 30%–35% 的资金争夺比例。美联储拦不住这个。他们其实无能为力，因为这帮人不管什么利率都会借钱——6%、8%、10%、12% 都借。

turns.en: It doesn't matter. They're in an existential race to figure out what's going to happen. If you remember back to the original .com boom, all those companies there, you might have 10 companies all working in one small area, one of them won.
turns.zh: 无所谓。他们正处在一场关乎存亡的竞赛里，要弄清最后会发生什么。如果你回想当初的互联网（.com）泡沫，那么多公司，可能在一个小领域里有 10 家公司在做，最后只有一家胜出。

turns.en: Now, did you know which one was going to be? No, the pets.com win? No, they didn't, but some other pet company might have won. And so these people here are fighting it out.
turns.zh: 那么，你当时知道会是哪一家吗？不知道。是 pets.com 赢了吗？不，但他们也没料到，可能是另一家宠物公司赢了。所以现在这些人正在厮杀。

turns.en: And I don't think there's a price where they will stop borrowing to go build out their systems. Harley, I'm going to ask you to take a tangent with me here because obviously everybody knows you are Mr. Fixed Income, inventor of the move index and so forth.
turns.zh: 我不觉得存在某个价格，能让他们停止借钱去搭建自己的系统。——Harley，我要请你跟我岔开一下话题，因为显然大家都知道你是“固定收益先生”，是 MOVE 指数的发明人等等。

turns.en: But I think this is so timely this week. You're a smart guy, so I just want to go in a totally different direction, a little bit outside your wheelhouse, which is, hey, this feud that started this week where Dario Amodi and other people said we have to slow down AI.
turns.zh: 但我觉得这件事本周太应景了。你是个聪明人，所以我只想往一个完全不同的方向走，稍微超出你的专长范围，就是——嘿，本周开始的这场论战，Dario Amodei 和其他一些人说我们必须放慢 AI 的发展。

turns.en: At first, everybody thought, oh, my God, this is the catalyst that's going to crash the bubble in the AI and, you know, all the hyperscaler debt.
turns.zh: 一开始，大家都想，天哪，这就是那个催化剂，会戳破 AI 的泡沫，还有，你知道，所有超大规模云厂商的债务。

turns.en: It's all going to crash. It's, you know, this is the end. And then President Trump came out incredibly strongly, actually phoning in to the all in podcast live event saying full steam ahead.
turns.zh: 全都要崩盘了，你知道，这就是末日。然后 Trump 总统极其强硬地站了出来，甚至打电话到 All-In 播客的现场活动，说全速前进。

turns.en: Don't listen. I think he actually had some strong, personally critical language about some of the people that were raising other concerns and it's very, very strong between President Trump and his economic advisor, David Sacks, that it's full steam ahead on AI.
turns.zh: 别听他们的。我觉得他其实用了一些很重的、带人身批评意味的话，去说那些提出其他担忧的人；而且在 Trump 总统和他的经济顾问 David Sacks 之间，态度非常非常明确：AI 就是要全速前进。

turns.en: We're not going to regulate anything and we're not going to let these, you know, left-wing nutcase pansies in San Francisco tell us what to do was at least the way I interpreted it.
turns.zh: 我们什么都不会去监管，也不会让旧金山那些左翼疯子和软蛋来告诉我们该怎么做——至少我是这么解读的。

turns.en: Is this the beginning of something that could really unwind the AI trade? Or is this just another political spectacle that's going to pass? I think the latter, look, just because there's no specific law about something doesn't mean you can't do the right thing anyways.
turns.zh: 这是不是某件可能真正瓦解 AI 交易的事情的开端？还是只是又一场终将过去的政治闹剧？——我觉得是后者。听着，就算某件事没有具体的法律约束，也不代表你就不能去做正确的事。

turns.en: And I do think that the AI people have recognized there's there could be a problem here. I'm not a believer that we're going to have the end of civilization in 10 years.
turns.zh: 我确实认为，AI 那帮人已经意识到这里可能存在问题。我不相信我们会在 10 年内迎来文明的终结。

turns.en: I did see the movie in the 70s. It did not end well, but I don't think it's going to happen. I do think it's possible that these are smart people who I assume some of them have an interest in the country overall, a little bit of patriotism and a little bit of concern for the world overall.
turns.zh: 我确实看过 70 年代那部电影，结局并不好，但我不觉得那会发生。我确实认为，这些人是聪明的，我猜他们中有一些人是对整个国家有责任感、有点爱国心、也有点关心整个世界的人。

turns.en: Yeah, there's a problem of what if China does it first or Russia or North Korea? I guess that exists, but I think it's possible to find a middle ground here where you don't have to go full steam ahead.
turns.zh: 是的，存在一个问题：万一中国先做出来，或者俄罗斯、朝鲜呢？我想这个问题确实存在，但我觉得这里有可能找到一个中间地带，让你不必全速前进。

turns.en: And I suspect that there will be some internal controls, even despite various political wailings. And as a fixed income guy, how do you feel about this unprecedented?
turns.zh: 我猜即便有各种政治上的哀嚎，还是会出现一些内部管控。——那么，作为一个固定收益人，你怎么看这种前所未有的局面？

turns.en: I think it might have, I don't remember, your slide deck or somewhere else. I saw this recently. I think the size of the AI and hyperscaler related debt is now bigger than the municipal bond market or something like that.
turns.zh: 我记得好像在你的幻灯片里，或者别的什么地方——我最近看到这个。我觉得 AI 和超大规模云厂商相关债务的规模，现在已经比市政债（municipal bond）市场还大，或者差不多那个量级。

turns.en: I don't remember the statistic, but it was staggering. Is there something could go wrong here? I don't think so. I think can we get higher rates because of their borrowing?
turns.zh: 我记不清那个数据了，但它大得惊人。——这里会不会出什么问题？我不觉得。我认为，我们会不会因为他们的借款而迎来更高的利率？

turns.en: Yes, but these guys have, most of them have underlying cash machines. They can certainly cover the cost of the debt. And I'm pretty sure unless there's a major standard oil kind of breakup of these companies that they have the ability to go and pay off these debts eventually.
turns.zh: 会，但这帮公司里，大多数都有底层的现金机器。他们当然能覆盖债务成本。而且我很确定，除非出现类似当年 Standard Oil 那样的大拆分，否则他们最终有能力还清这些债务。

turns.en: Now, that doesn't mean the equity holders are going to do well. Profits might go down because of the spending. So the equity I can't comment on, but I think the bonds are probably money good.
turns.zh: 不过，这并不意味着股东会赚得好。利润可能因为这些支出而下降。所以股票我不好评论，但我觉得这些债券大概率是“钱稳的”（money good，即本息无虞）。

turns.en: And if you tack on another 50, 100, 200 basis points, I think it's fine. I just don't see a bankruptcy with the hyperscalers. They all have underlying core businesses that are very profitable.
turns.zh: 就算再加上 50、100、200 个基点，我觉得也没问题。我就是看不到超大规模云厂商会破产。它们都有非常赚钱的底层核心业务。

turns.en: Wait a minute. I don't think of the AI companies like Anthropic as being very profitable from the standpoint that really they're subsidizing a lot of their operations.
turns.zh: 等一下。我不认为像 Anthropic 这样的 AI 公司很赚钱，从某种意义上说，它们的很多运营其实是在靠补贴撑着。

turns.en: Barry told us last week that the risk in this whole AI market is China giving it away for free, which was Google's tactic back in the 90s that really eliminated a lot of competition.
turns.zh: Barry 上周告诉我们，整个 AI 市场的风险在于中国把它免费送出，而这正是 Google 在 90 年代用过、真正消灭了很多竞争对手的招数。

turns.en: And the way that plays out is Chinese AI models that are almost as good as Anthropic's best models get open sourced. And if you buy your own hardware, which also gives you the advantage of protecting the privacy of your data, you suddenly don't need Anthropic anymore because the free stuff from China is just as good.
turns.zh: 而它的演绎方式是，中国的 AI 模型——几乎和 Anthropic 最好的模型一样好——被开源。如果你自己买硬件（这还顺带给你保护数据隐私的好处），你突然间就不再需要 Anthropic 了，因为来自中国的免费东西一样好。

turns.en: Now, that hasn't happened quite yet. But if it did, doesn't that put a lot of this industry at risk in terms of its ability to service that debt?
turns.zh: 当然，这还没完全发生。但如果真发生了，难道不会让整个行业在偿债能力上陷入很大风险吗？

turns.en: Look, Anthropic is not borrowing the money. The other guys are borrowing the money to use Anthropic's products. So because Anthropic go bust, I sure.
turns.zh: 听着，Anthropic 并不是那个借钱的人。是其他公司在借钱来使用 Anthropic 的产品。所以就算 Anthropic 破产，我当然……

turns.en: But that's an equity problem, not a bond problem. And I think the hyperscalers, I think Meta, Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Oracle, they have plenty of cashflow coming on through to fund, to make the coupon payments that pay these things back over time.
turns.zh: 但那是股票的问题，不是债券的问题。而且我觉得那些超大规模云厂商——Meta、Google、Amazon、Microsoft、Oracle——它们有源源不断的充裕现金流，去支付票息、并随时间把这些债务还掉。

turns.en: It doesn't mean their stocks not going to go down. But I think the bonds are solid. Okay. And it certainly makes sense that, as you say, they're running Anthropic stuff.
turns.zh: 这不代表它们的股票不会跌。但我觉得债券是稳的。——好。而且正如你说的，它们是在跑 Anthropic 的东西，这一点确实说得通。

turns.en: So if we get to a point, as Matt Barry is predicting, where Chinese open source AI models are really just as good and you can get it almost for free, that just reduces the cost of those hyperscalers.
turns.zh: 所以，如果像 Matt Barry 预测的那样，我们真到了那一步——中国开源 AI 模型确实一样好、而且你几乎能免费拿到——那只会降低那些超大规模云厂商的成本。

turns.en: You know, they're not paying nearly as much as they used to pay Anthropic. They're getting it lower. They're more able to service their debt.
turns.zh: 你知道，它们不用再像过去付给 Anthropic 那么多钱了。它们拿到手的成本更低，也就更有能力偿还债务。

turns.en: Is that kind of the way you see it playing out? All you're saying to me is global crossing from 25 years ago, redux, right? They laid the cable out there and they thought they'd get X dollars per megabyte and they turned out to be one tenth of that and that happened.
turns.zh: 你大致是这么看它的发展吗？——你跟我说的一切，其实就是 25 年前 Global Crossing 的重演，对吧？他们把光缆铺出去，以为每兆字节能收 X 美元，结果只有那个的十分之一，事情就是这么发生的。

turns.en: So yeah, these four guys, five hyperscalers, I mean, one of them is going to go and win and maybe two of them, but the rest of them are going to have a problem because most markets tend towards a monopoly.
turns.zh: 所以是的，这四家、五家超大规模云厂商，我是说，其中一家会胜出，也许两家，但剩下的都会出问题，因为大多数市场都趋向于垄断。

turns.en: It's just the natural course of things, which is why you have antitrust rules. That's why we used to have, you know, a dozen stocks changes.
turns.zh: 这就是事物的自然规律，所以才有了反垄断规则。这也是为什么我们过去有，你知道，十几家证券交易所。

turns.en: Now we have one or two. I think the same thing happens here. You're going to have only a few winners, not everybody. And that's why they're so desperate to raise money and build themselves out, hoping they're the winner.
turns.zh: 现在只剩一两家了。我觉得这里也会发生同样的事。最终只会有少数几个赢家，而不是所有人。这就是为什么他们如此拼命地融资、扩张自己，指望着自己就是那个赢家。

turns.en: I'm not sure they know they're the winner yet. Well, thanks for taking that tangent out of your core expertise. Let's return to that core expertise here on page 10.
turns.zh: 我还不确定他们自己知道谁是赢家。——好，谢谢你陪我岔开话题、聊了这些你核心专长之外的东西。我们回到你的核心专长，看第 10 页。

turns.en: Oh my gosh, US debt as a percent of GDP is actually going up. How about that? Look, you could look at page 10, page 11. There's nothing new under the sun over here in terms of debt to GDP or the fiscal deficit.
turns.zh: 天哪，美国债务占 GDP 的比重居然还在往上走，你说怪不怪？——听着，你可以看第 10 页、第 11 页。就债务对 GDP 或财政赤字而言，这边太阳底下没有新鲜事。

turns.en: Let's really hit on what's important is I've been building up this idea of, I don't care about the numbers. I care about trust. Okay. Page 12 is where the weather meets the road.
turns.zh: 我们真正要敲的重点是，我一直在铺垫这个观点：我不在乎那些数字，我在乎的是信任。好，第 12 页才是见真章的地方。

turns.en: We've had rates go up 150 bits, which is a pretty big number considering where we started at and the break even inflation rate between tips and nominal treasuries is 235 on average for the last four years.
turns.zh: 利率已经上行了 150 个基点（bps），考虑到我们的起点，这是个相当大的数字；而过去四年，TIPS（通胀保值债券）与名义国债之间的盈亏平衡通胀率（breakeven inflation rate）平均为 2.35%。

turns.en: And by the way, I checked my Bloomberg before I started this show and we closed at a 234 spread for a 10 year inflation. That's kind of crazy town because what it's telling you is inflation.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，我在录这期节目前查了我的 Bloomberg，10 年期通胀的利差收在 2.34%。这有点离谱，因为它告诉你的是，通胀……

turns.en: No, it cares about inflation, right? If they cared about inflation, they thought inflation was the problem. That's what's driving the whole market and the volatility and insanity.
turns.zh: 不，没人在乎通胀，对吧？如果他们在乎通胀、认为通胀才是问题所在，那才是驱动整个市场、驱动那些波动与疯狂的东西。

turns.en: That spread would widen. It's not. It tells you we're looking in the wrong place. And that's why I keep saying it's about building trust in the Fed and the Treasury that these now going back, I guess, as slides 10 and 11, we have a fiscal problem that's just out of control.
turns.zh: 那个利差本该走阔。可它没有。这告诉你，我们找错了地方。这也是为什么我一直说，关键在于建立对美联储和财政部的信任——现在回到，我想是第 10 和第 11 张幻灯片，我们有一个已经完全失控的财政问题。

turns.en: We're running a 6% deficit. We're not at war. We're not in a recession. We only have 4.1, 4.2 unemployment. Things are grand and we're running a 6% deficit.
turns.zh: 我们正运行着 6% 的赤字。我们没在打仗，也没陷入衰退，失业率只有 4.1%、4.2%。一切都好得很，可我们却在跑 6% 的赤字。

turns.en: This is just beyond, it is gross irresponsibility. And this is, and this is what we're seeing now is that all these rates are rising because people are starting to be concerned about the US as a going concern, not a bankruptcy, because we can always print the money as a going concern of holding US dollars as a core asset and what it costs to own, what rate I want to take to own dollars.
turns.zh: 这简直是……这是极其不负责任。而我们现在看到的，就是所有这些利率都在上升，因为人们开始担心美国作为一个持续经营主体（going concern）的问题——不是破产，因为我们总能印钱——而是把美元作为核心资产持有这个“持续经营”的问题，以及持有它的成本、我要收多高的利率才愿意持有美元。

turns.en: Okay. You've got me obsessed now with slide 12, because I really want to understand your intended meaning. I agree with you that 234 is telling us, you know, the tips discount is not really concerned about inflation, but it seems to me that there's a huge amount of concern about inflation just in terms of the narratives that you hear.
turns.zh: 好。你现在让我对第 12 页着迷了，因为我真的很想理解你要表达的意思。我同意你说的，2.34% 在告诉我们，TIPS 的折价其实并不真的担心通胀；但在我看来，光从你听到的各种叙事来看，就有大量对通胀的担忧。

turns.en: You're Mr. Data, you invented the move index. When we see that disparity, I'm tempted to say, okay, this slide 12 is telling us inflation is not the concern that the market is worried about.
turns.zh: 你是“数据先生”，你发明了 MOVE 指数。当我们看到这种背离时，我很想说，好，第 12 页在告诉我们，通胀并不是市场真正担心的那个问题。

turns.en: I should stop worrying about inflation. It's not going to be a problem. But then I think, wait a minute, aren't tips completely based on the CPI?
turns.zh: 我该停止担心通胀了，它不会成为问题。但转念一想，等等，TIPS 不完全是基于 CPI 的吗？

turns.en: And a lot of people have criticized the CPI doesn't really accurately reflect inflation. You know, is there a possibility that this is not really an accurate signal that we're following here?
turns.zh: 而且很多人批评说 CPI 并不能真正准确反映通胀。你知道，有没有可能我们在追踪的这个信号其实并不准确？

turns.en: I think you have stumbled over the truth that maybe CPI is not the right answer for inflation, that CPI has been rigged for 30 years after they rejiggered it during Clinton, and when they put in hedonics and everything else, it was a public policy goal to reduce stated CPI.
turns.zh: 我觉得你无意中撞见了真相：CPI 也许并不是衡量通胀的正确答案；自从 Clinton 时期他们把 CPI 重新调整、引入享乐调整（hedonics）等等之后，CPI 已经被“做手脚”30 年了，当时的公共政策目标就是要压低公布的 CPI。

turns.en: So the expenditure of Social Security would be lower. And so, yes, I had a fine idea and CPI is, is it cooked a little bit, but if they keep talking CPI in the Fed meetings, right, I mean, the core or everything else, I mean, they're kind of using that as, as, as their metric of risk and value.
turns.zh: 这样社会保障（Social Security）的支出就会更低。所以，是的，我有这么个想法——CPI 是不是被“烹制”过一点？但如果他们在美联储会议上还是一直谈 CPI，我是说，核心 CPI 或其他什么的，那他们其实就是在拿它当作衡量风险和价值的指标。

turns.en: So maybe they know better, maybe they don't. But I think there's, I think there's something else going on here. We need to go and recognize what that is.
turns.zh: 所以也许他们心里有数，也许没有。但我觉得，这里还有别的东西在起作用。我们需要去认清那到底是什么。

turns.en: I propose the idea of trust doesn't mean I'm right, but I just, we're not seeing this idea that CPI is the driver of nominal rates going higher right here, and maybe some of your other experts will come on in a week or two or three, explain why this chart is totally meaningless, and I'll accept them as being right.
turns.zh: 我提出“信任”这个说法，并不意味着我就是对的，只是——我们并没有在这里看到“CPI 是推高名义利率的驱动因素”这个逻辑；也许一两周或三周后，你们的其他专家会上节目，解释为什么这张图毫无意义，那我也会承认他们是对的。

turns.en: But it does not seem to be inflation is what's taking us higher, causing problems over here. Well, we have lots of experts who love to, to pick her with Harley Baspin just because of your reputation having invented the move index.
turns.zh: 但看起来，把利率推高、在这边制造问题的，并不是通胀。——我们有好多专家都喜欢跟 Harley Bassman 较劲，就因为你发明了 MOVE 指数、名气在外。

turns.en: I just want to close on slide 12 and make sure I've got it though. You're saying that your interpretation of slide 12 is look what the market's most reliable indicator, even though it might be somewhat colored by the fact that CPI is not accurate.
turns.zh: 我只想在第 12 页上收个尾，确认我真的理解了。你是说，你对第 12 页的解读是：看，市场最可靠的那个指标——尽管它可能因为 CPI 不准确而带了些杂色——

turns.en: The indicator that we have is telling us that all these narratives that sound pretty darn plausible about why we should be very concerned about inflation getting worse and potentially runaway bond yields and all the things that come with it.
turns.zh: 我们手上的这个指标在告诉我们，所有这些听起来相当言之有理的叙事——说什么我们该非常担心通胀恶化、债券收益率可能失控，以及随之而来的一切——

turns.en: The market is telling us that just plain ain't happening. Is that the right way to interpret slide 12? It does look that way, doesn't it? Yeah, that's kind of it.
turns.zh: 市场在告诉我们，那些事根本就没在发生。——这是解读第 12 页的正确方式吗？——看起来确实是这样，不是吗？是的，大致就是这个意思。

turns.en: We should be seeing nominals go up versus tips. It all was fine and dandy and it was inflation that was driving interest rates. Okay. One of the things that you've talked to us quite a bit about in your past interviews has been mortgage backed securities and where the opportunities exist in those markets.
turns.zh: 如果一切正常、真的是通胀在驱动利率，那我们本该看到名义国债相对 TIPS 上行。好。你在过去的访谈里跟我们聊得相当多的一件事，是抵押贷款支持证券（mortgage-backed securities），以及这些市场里的机会在哪里。

turns.en: So let's move on to page 13. I published a commentary about the mortgage convexity beast raising its head. It's a great story. I mean, I invented the convexity vortex, I don't know, 25 years ago.
turns.zh: 那我们翻到第 13 页。我发表过一篇评论，讲的是抵押贷款凸性这头野兽正抬起头来。这是个很好的故事。我是说，“凸性漩涡”（convexity vortex）就是我发明的，大概在 25 年前吧。

turns.en: Remember, what is a mortgage? A mortgage bond is a simply a covered call. You could model it up by saying I buy a cash 10 year at par. I sell a call, a three year call struck at 105 and that's the package.
turns.zh: 记住，什么是抵押贷款？一只抵押贷款债券其实就是一个备兑看涨（covered call）。你可以这样建模：我按面值买入一只 10 年期现券，再卖出一个行权价 105 的 3 年期看涨期权，这就是整个组合。

turns.en: There's no credit risk in mortgage bonds. Fannie, Freddie, Jenny, if you think they're going to go down my humble advice is gold guns and cans of tuna because that's what you're going to need if any Freddie go bankrupt and how they're valued.
turns.zh: 抵押贷款债券没有信用风险。Fannie、Freddie、Ginnie，如果你觉得它们会倒，那我的拙见是去囤黄金、枪支和金枪鱼罐头，因为一旦哪家 Freddie 破产，那就是你会用到的东西——以及它们会如何被重新定价。

turns.en: The spread you get over treasuries has to do with the probability of the possibility of these bonds being called. Right. And if you are in a covered call strategy, that means your downside's unlimited because that's protected from going south and your upside is capped out at 105.
turns.zh: 你相对国债拿到的利差，与这些债券被赎回（called）的可能性概率有关。对吧。而如果你处在一个备兑看涨策略里，那意味着你的下行是无限的——因为下行其实被保护着不至于往下走——而你的上行则封顶在 105。

turns.en: And the example I've given you what we had three years ago. Looking at slide 13, is it 71% of the market at a three and a half percent coupon or lower?
turns.zh: 我给你举个例子，就是三年前我们的情况。看第 13 页，是不是有 71% 的市场票息在 3.5% 或更低？

turns.en: It wasn't public policy good to force people or help people refinance their mortgages. There of course been unintended consequences we could talk about later, but this was a public policy good to help people lock in these low rates.
turns.zh: 从公共政策角度看，推动或帮助人们再融资（refinance）他们的抵押贷款是好事。当然这带来了一些意外后果，我们稍后可以谈，但从公共政策看，帮人们锁定这些低利率是好事。

turns.en: So the advantage of this QE, which is suspect, was spread around to ordinary people. The mortgage market at the time was actually theoretically long optionality, believe it or not, because most of the market was trading at a dollar price of 82 and lower.
turns.zh: 所以那种（本身可疑的）QE 的好处，被分摊给了普通老百姓。信不信由你，当时的抵押贷款市场其实在理论上是“做多期权性”（long optionality）的，因为市场上大部分都以 82 或更低的美元价格在交易。

turns.en: As you're having, you could look at the slide, the blue column and the average price of the 30 year mortgage market, Jenny, Fanny, Freddie was $79, 78, 90, 40 per slice.
turns.zh: 你可以看这张幻灯片，那根蓝色柱子，30 年期抵押贷款市场（Ginnie、Fannie、Freddie）的平均价格，当时是每档 79、78、90.40 美元。

turns.en: That's a pretty far away from the price of 105 as an exercise price. So the market did not have that much convexity to it and trader built only tight to treasuries because the optionality was so small.
turns.zh: 这离 105 这个行权价相当远。所以市场并没有太多凸性，交易员们只是紧贴着国债报价，因为期权性实在太小了。

turns.en: What has happened in the last three years is what's called recouponing the stack, recouponing the stack. The stack is all those coupons. And by recouponing, we basically see the low coupon bonds going away, either because the principal is being paid down or because there's a refinancing or because there's a divorce, grandma dies, you move or anything that could cause a mortgage bond to prepay and the new bonds are being produced or higher coupon.
turns.zh: 过去三年发生的，是所谓的“票息结构再重置”（recouponing the stack）。这个“stack”指的是所有这些票息档。通过再重置，我们基本上看到低票息的债券在消失——要么是因为本金在被偿还，要么是因为再融资，要么是因为离婚、奶奶去世、你搬家，或任何可能导致抵押贷款债券提前偿付（prepay）的原因——而新产生的债券票息更高。

turns.en: And you can see you now have over a trillion Fanny five and a halfs that exist on the bottom section of page 13. Now, so we've recouponed. So now we only have 51 52% of low coupon mortgages in the overall mortgage index and 37% for the five coupon or higher.
turns.zh: 你可以看到，现在在第 13 页下半部分，存在超过 1 万亿的 Fannie 5.5% 债券。所以，我们已经完成了票息再重置。现在整个抵押贷款指数里，低票息抵押贷款只占 51%–52%，而票息 5% 或更高的占 37%。

turns.en: These bonds are all very negatively convex. An option is most convex when it's at strike. The option is most convex when it's at strike. And remember, let me define convexity again.
turns.zh: 这些债券全都是高度负凸性（negatively convex）的。一个期权在处于行权价（at strike）时凸性最大。期权在处于行权价时凸性最大。记住，让我再定义一次凸性。

turns.en: Convexity means unbalanced return. So if I have a bet, I can make a dollar or lose a dollar on a coin flip. That's zero convexity. If I could make two, lose one, positive convexity.
turns.zh: 凸性意味着不对称的收益。所以如果我有一个赌注，抛硬币要么赚 1 美元要么亏 1 美元，那就是零凸性。如果我能赚 2、亏 1，那就是正凸性。

turns.en: If I could lose three, make two, negative convexity. That's all convexity means is just looking at the relative balance going up and down on something.
turns.zh: 如果我亏 3、赚 2，那就是负凸性。凸性说来说去，就是看一个东西上涨和下跌之间的相对平衡。

turns.en: And then what the market does is it prices it out. So if I have an ordinary bond yields 5% with zero convexity, so a point down a point. Please don't geniuses out there.
turns.zh: 然后市场所做的，就是给它定价。所以如果我有一只普通债券，收益率 5%、零凸性，也就是涨一个点跌一个点。请各位“天才”先别急——

turns.en: Yes, I know bonds all positive convexity. Ignore that for now. Regular tenure. If I have a bond next to it that goes up, up two down one, that's a better bond.
turns.zh: 是的，我知道债券都有正凸性。先忽略这一点。就普通的 10 年期而言。如果我旁边还有一只债券，涨 2 跌 1，那就是一只更好的债券。

turns.en: And therefore I'll take a lower yield four and a half, four, three and a half. I don't know something like that, but it's a better bond. So it can't be the same yield.
turns.zh: 因此我会接受一个更低的收益率，4.5%、4%、3.5%，我也说不准，大概这样，但它是更好的债券。所以它的收益率不可能和那只一样。

turns.en: And what all these geniuses do is they figure out how much should the yield be above or below 5% to compensate for the embedded option. If I have another bond that is down three, up two, that's a lesser bond.
turns.zh: 而那些“天才”们做的，就是算出收益率应该在 5% 之上或之下多少，来补偿那个内嵌期权（embedded option）。如果我有另一只债券是跌 3、涨 2，那就是一只更差的债券。

turns.en: I'll need to get a higher yield versus the 5% Treasury to make me want to buy it. In this case over here, that extra spread is what a mortgage bond looks like.
turns.zh: 我就需要相对 5% 的国债拿到更高的收益率，才愿意去买它。而在这边这个情形里，那份额外的利差，就是一只抵押贷款债券的样子。

turns.en: And right now it's about 110 basis points over Treasuries. Now, what drives that 110? Well, you can go to page 14 and that shows you the mortgage bond spread.
turns.zh: 现在它大约是高于国债 110 个基点。那么，是什么驱动了这 110？你可以翻到第 14 页，它给你展示了抵押贷款债券的利差。

turns.en: Par mortgage bond, a mortgage bond trading at 100 versus the cash tenure. And you can see it goes up and out, up and down. Right now it's, this slide's a few days old, it's now 110.
turns.zh: 面值抵押贷款债券——也就是一只以 100 交易的抵押贷款债券——对比 10 年期现券。你可以看到它上上下下。现在，这张幻灯片已经几天了，如今是 110。

turns.en: It's widening out. It's widening up for two reasons. One, everyone knows. Volatility has gone up since you're short an option. If volatility goes up, the option goes up and you're short the option here.
turns.zh: 它在走阔。走阔有两个原因。第一个大家都知道：波动率上升了，因为你是做空期权的一方。波动率上升，期权价值上升，而你在这里是做空期权的。

turns.en: So the spread widens. Let me tell you the trick. What's more important than that right now. The yield curve. This is very technical. I'm just going to make the statement to you.
turns.zh: 所以利差走阔。让我告诉你那个窍门，也是当下更重要的东西：收益率曲线。这非常技术性，我就直接给你个结论。

turns.en: When the yield curve flattens or inverts mortgage bonds, widen. The option becomes worth more and mortgage bonds become more negatively convex.
turns.zh: 当收益率曲线变平或倒挂时，抵押贷款债券的利差就会走阔。期权变得更值钱，抵押贷款债券也就变得更负凸。

turns.en: And what you've seen happening right in the last month over here, two months, three months is the yield curve flattening. And so mortgage bonds are becoming more negatively convex.
turns.zh: 而你在过去一个月、两个月、三个月里看到的，就是收益率曲线在变平。所以抵押贷款债券正变得越来越负凸。

turns.en: And that's why you have this wider spread. From basically mid 95 to 110. And if the curve keeps inverting, it's going to get worse. And so the mortgage market is going to start to have an impact on the overall fixed income market because the mortgage market makes up a quarter of the, of all issuance out there.
turns.zh: 这就是为什么利差会更宽，基本上从 95 附近走阔到了 110。而如果曲线继续倒挂，情况还会更糟。所以抵押贷款市场将开始对整个固定收益市场产生影响，因为抵押贷款市场占了全部发行量的四分之一。

turns.en: It'll become important. It's not as important as it was 20 years ago when Fannie and Freddie, basically government sponsored hedge funds were running the deck, but it will be important.
turns.zh: 它会变得重要。虽然不像 20 年前那么重要——那时 Fannie 和 Freddie，基本上是政府支持的对冲基金，主宰着整个局面。但它会变得重要。

turns.en: So watch out for and if you're involved in the mortgage market, yeah, be careful. If you're looking at the big index ETFs, the good news is this, is that they're going to go down quickly, but soon enough, they're just going to follow treasuries, the convexity will go away because as the price goes down, the option becomes worth less, you're further from strike, less convexity.
turns.zh: 所以要当心，如果你参与抵押贷款市场，是的，要小心。如果你看的是那些大型指数 ETF，好消息是：它们会先快速下跌，但用不了多久，它们就只会跟着国债走，凸性会消失，因为随着价格下跌，期权变得不值钱，你离行权价更远，凸性就更小。

turns.en: So the mortgage market will act more consistently. So that's, I guess, a good news. Of course, your price will be lower by a lot, but the speed will slow down.
turns.zh: 所以抵押贷款市场的表现会更一致。这，我想，算是个好消息。当然，你的价格会低很多，但下跌的速度会慢下来。

turns.en: Harley, I'm going to ask you to entertain another tangent because I'm absolutely fascinated by where this AI stuff is headed. Look, what you've just said in the insight, we're just scratching at the surface of your knowledge here.
turns.zh: Harley，我要请你再陪我岔开一个话题，因为我完全被 AI 这些东西的走向迷住了。听着，你刚才说的那些洞见——我们在这里不过是浅尝了你知识的皮毛。

turns.en: The reason you've earned this industry wide moniker of the convexity maven is you've got really strong expertise and you've generated a lot of alpha during your career.
turns.zh: 你之所以赢得“凸性专家”（Convexity Maven）这个行业内的绰号，是因为你有非常过硬的专长，而且在你职业生涯中创造了大量的 alpha（超额收益）。

turns.en: You've made a lot of money for you and your clients. You've got a lot to be proud of, but hang on a second. Every word that we're saying in this podcast is being transcripted at macrovoices.com and it will be two days before it's been sucked into every AI training model in the world.
turns.zh: 你为自己和客户赚了很多钱，有很多值得骄傲的地方。但且慢——我们在这档播客里说的每一个字，都会被转录到 macrovoices.com，用不了两天，就会被世界上每一个 AI 训练模型吸进去。

turns.en: They've also already consumed every other word you've ever said publicly, every page you've ever written during the course of your career and every colleague that's ever had an opinion on anything.
turns.zh: 它们也早就吞下了你公开说过的每一个字、你职业生涯中写过的每一页东西，以及每一位曾对任何事发表过看法的同行。

turns.en: It's all in AI. Already, we've had lesser guys than you in terms of intellect really beginning to be able to compete with you because AI is helping them.
turns.zh: 这些全都进了 AI。已经有那些在智力上不如你的人，真的开始能和你竞争了，因为 AI 在帮他们。

turns.en: That's only the AI assist of humans level and what's really happening right now in the AI market is this transition towards a genetic AI where you wouldn't have so-called algorithmic trading, just doing simplistic stuff like, you know, mean reversion to scalpa trade that happened in the last 10 seconds in high-frequency trading, but you'd have AI models that are just as smart as you because they've read every word you ever said and every word that your
turns.zh: 那还只是“AI 辅助人类”的层面。而 AI 市场现在真正在发生的，是向通用 AI（general AI）的转变：你不会再有所谓的算法交易，只做那些简单的东西，比如均值回归（mean reversion）、在高频交易里去剥头皮（scalp）过去 10 秒发生的一笔交易；你会拥有和你一样聪明的 AI 模型，因为它们读过你说过的每一个字、你的

turns.en: colleagues ever said and they've compared it against every bit of market data that's ever existed. Do we get to a point where all of the alpha generation capacity that markets have is completely consumed by AI and it's possible, it becomes impossible for human traders to ever compete with them?
turns.zh: 同行们说过的每一个字，还把这些和历史上存在过的每一点市场数据做了比对。我们会不会走到那样一步：市场所有的 alpha 生成能力都被 AI 完全吃掉，以至于人类交易员根本不可能再与它们竞争？

turns.en: I suppose if you told me that you went to China, used their best model and typed in, what is Warsh going to do at two o'clock New York time?
turns.zh: 我想，如果你告诉我，你跑到中国，用他们最好的模型，然后输入：“Warsh 在纽约时间两点会怎么做？”

turns.en: I suppose you'd be right, but I don't buy that quite yet. These models still can't predict the future. What they can do is create the best portfolio given a set of parameters and then react as the news comes out.
turns.zh: 我想你可能是对的，但我现在还不太信。这些模型仍然无法预测未来。它们能做的，是在给定一组参数的情况下构建最优的组合，然后在消息出来时做出反应。

turns.en: And there are plenty of systems out there that look at key words from the Fed or from the news and they trade on that, which is fine. But they're not predicting the number, they're reacting to the number.
turns.zh: 外面有大量系统会盯着美联储或新闻里的关键词，然后据此交易，这没问题。但它们不是在预测那个数字，而是在对那个数字做出反应。

turns.en: And so until we go and we could know in advance what's going to happen, I think humans are going to do just fine with all this. Now, will they be able to perform better?
turns.zh: 所以，在我们能够事先知道将会发生什么之前，我觉得人类在这一切面前会过得挺好。那么，他们能不能表现得更好呢？

turns.en: That's interesting actually if you think about it. I guess you're kind of turning over the rock of what happens if we eventually have all portfolio management go to AI systems.
turns.zh: 仔细想想，这其实很有意思。我猜你是在掀开一块石头：如果我们最终把所有的组合管理都交给 AI 系统，会发生什么？

turns.en: In theory, there'd be no money to be made at all because everyone would have the most efficient result, right? Right. And the way I'm looking at this is everybody knows we haven't quite arrived at this moment called artificial general intelligence where AI becomes better than humans at most things.
turns.zh: 理论上，那就根本无钱可赚了，因为每个人都会得到最高效的结果，对吧？对。——我看这件事的角度是：大家都知道，我们还没真正抵达那个叫通用人工智能（artificial general intelligence）的时刻，也就是 AI 在大多数事情上都比人类强的时刻。

turns.en: But almost everybody agrees that's coming and coming really soon. And furthermore, the acceleration actually increases through that point to where AI becomes smarter than any human pretty darn quickly, maybe within the next year.
turns.zh: 但几乎所有人都同意它正在到来，而且来得很快。更重要的是，那个加速度在越过该点后其实还会加大，快到 AI 会相当迅速地比任何人类都聪明，也许就在未来一年之内。

turns.en: So at that point, how do you sell your two and 20 fee structure as a service if there's AI that can beat you consistently? And as you said, if the AI gets really, really good, which seems to me could be coming in the next five years, all the AI outcompetes itself and all of a sudden there is no alpha in the market, but everybody has to rely on AI in order to not lose badly.
turns.zh: 所以到了那个时候，如果有 AI 能持续打败你，你还怎么把“2 加 20”（two and 20）的收费结构当作服务卖出去？而且正如你说的，如果 AI 变得非常非常好——在我看来这可能在未来五年内到来——所有的 AI 互相竞争到彼此超越，突然间市场上就没有 alpha 了，但每个人都必须依赖 AI 才不至于输得很惨。

turns.en: Seems like there's a lot of crazy stuff that could happen. Seems to me you're slowly digging into the whole idea of passive investing and why one does it because they can't beat the market anymore or the active guys can't beat the market in equities.
turns.zh: 看起来可能会发生很多疯狂的事。在我看来，你是在慢慢挖向被动投资（passive investing）这整个理念——以及人们为什么做被动投资：因为他们再也打不赢市场了，或者说做主动的那帮人在股票上打不赢市场了。

turns.en: So they're going into passive, which is another whole can of worms out there about my friend, your friend, Michael Green, his whole gig on passive and how that's working in the market and driving everything, which by the way, I think Mike's right.
turns.zh: 所以他们转向被动，而这又打开了另一个潘多拉魔盒——关于我的朋友、也是你的朋友 Michael Green，他那整套关于被动投资的论述，讲它如何在市场里运作、驱动着一切。顺便说一句，我觉得 Mike 是对的。

turns.en: And as a free plug, I'll tell you, he's coming out with a new product that I think might be kind of interesting, but it's in registration now, so I can't talk about it.
turns.zh: 作为一次免费打广告，我告诉你，他正要推出一款新产品，我觉得可能挺有意思，但它现在处于注册（registration）阶段，所以我不能多谈。

turns.en: Wills are already turning in my mind. I want to ask the same question to Mike and we'll get him booked as soon as we can because he's definitely got a lot of perspective on this.
turns.zh: 我脑子里的齿轮已经在转了。我想把同样的问题也抛给 Mike，我们会尽快约到他，因为他在这件事上肯定有很多视角。

turns.en: And I've been very much in agreement with his statements about why passive is the risk and why going that passive strategy is not the right move.
turns.zh: 我一直非常认同他的说法——为什么被动本身就是风险，以及为什么采用那种被动策略并不是正确的招法。

turns.en: But boy, I think AI is going to change. I don't want to say necessarily change the outcome or make Mike wrong. But I got to believe Mike's already thinking a lot about this.
turns.zh: 但天哪，我觉得 AI 会带来改变。我不想说它一定会改变结果、或者让 Mike 说错。但我相信 Mike 已经在大量思考这个问题了。

turns.en: So we'll get that lined up. Well, if you want to go into drug land, are you talking about the idea that maybe AIs can go out there and scoop up all the raw data that the BLS gets, crank it out and know the CPI number before the CPI is released?
turns.zh: 所以我们会把那期安排上。——那么，如果你想天马行空地畅想，你说的是不是这样一个想法：也许 AI 能去把 BLS（劳工统计局）拿到的所有原始数据都扒过来，一通计算，然后在 CPI 公布之前就知道那个 CPI 数字？

turns.en: Is that what you're talking about now? No, I'm not necessarily talking about that. What I'm talking about is take the skill of yourself and every other trader who's ever been analyzed, take every word that Jack Schwager ever wrote in the Market Wizard series and start as a search the internet for everything more you can find out about the track record of all of those famous humans.
turns.zh: 你现在说的是这个吗？——不，我说的不一定是那个。我说的是：把你本人以及每一个被分析过的交易员的技能都拿来，把 Jack Schwager 在《金融怪杰》（Market Wizards）系列里写下的每一个字都拿来，再上网搜出所有你能找到的、关于那些名人交易业绩的资料。

turns.en: And basically tell AI your job is to generate alpha and beat the humans at it. And let AI figure out what it needs to do to do that by assimilating every skill you ever knew from your world of fixed income and every skill that Stan Druckenmiller ever knew from his world and every skill that every other famous trader ever knew and just be better at it than we humans are.
turns.zh: 然后基本上就是告诉 AI：你的任务是创造 alpha、并在这上面打败人类。让 AI 自己去想清楚该怎么做——把你从固定收益世界里掌握的每一项技能、Stan Druckenmiller 从他世界里掌握的每一项技能、以及其他每一位知名交易员掌握过的每一项技能全都吸收进来，然后做得比我们人类更好。

turns.en: At that point, already you have to be way better if you want to justify a hedge funds, you know, sized two and 20 fee structure, you've got to be better than the average human trader by a lot and you've got to be able to prove your history at generating alpha.
turns.zh: 到那时候，如果你想撑起一个对冲基金那种规模的“2 加 20”收费结构，你就必须远远更强，你得比一般的人类交易员好出一大截，而且你得能拿出你创造 alpha 的历史业绩来证明。

turns.en: Seems to me it's only a matter of time before one of the things that AI becomes better at than any human is generating alpha. My response to this near panic you're describing is a few of my comments.
turns.zh: 在我看来，AI 比任何人类都更擅长的事情之一变成“创造 alpha”，只是时间问题。——对你描述的这种近乎恐慌的情绪，我的回应是这么几点看法。

turns.en: Number one, it's always about character. And number two, it's never different this time. And they invented the car a hundred years ago and all the guys making saddles and buggy whips all managed to go and somehow survive.
turns.zh: 第一，这始终是关乎“特性”（character，人的本性）。第二，“这次不一样”从来都没兑现过。一百年前他们发明了汽车，而那些做马鞍和马车鞭的人，最后都设法活了下来。

turns.en: Maybe it took a while to do it. I would say that letting China in the WTO basically caused a disruption that the US government did not help by retraining people.
turns.zh: 也许花了一阵子。我会说，让中国加入 WTO 基本上造成了一次冲击，而美国政府并没有通过再培训人们来帮忙应对。

turns.en: But nonetheless, I mean, I think we'd survive that mostly. I tend to think that we're going to find a way to go and survive AI and use it as a tool to help civilization when we do have the ability to think creatively and we do have opposable thumbs, which AIs do not.
turns.zh: 但尽管如此，我是说，我觉得我们大体上还是熬过来了。我倾向于认为，我们会想办法在 AI 面前存活下来，并把它当作帮助文明的工具——毕竟我们确实有创造性思考的能力，也确实有可对握的拇指，而这些 AI 都没有。

turns.en: And I think I think that's kind of helpful. Let's move on to page 15 where you've got some projections about policy and other things. What's on your mind?
turns.zh: 我觉得这挺有帮助的。我们翻到第 15 页，你在上面有一些关于政策和其他事情的预测。你在想什么？

turns.en: Circling back to the idea it's not CPI, it's trust. And why is this trust being damaged? Because we have gross fiscal negligence running a six percent fiscal deficit in a world where not at war, a police action, I suppose, and not a recession.
turns.zh: 绕回到那个观点：问题不是 CPI，而是信任。为什么这份信任在受损？因为我们在财政上严重失职，在一个既没打仗（顶多算一次“警察行动”）、也没有衰退的世界里，却跑着 6% 的财政赤字。

turns.en: So somehow we got to pull this. We have to read to pull the spread down. What you're really seeing over here, just to take a little victory lap, is I was on this podcast a year or two or three or four ago when the MMT guys were all screaming and yelling how debt doesn't matter.
turns.zh: 所以我们得想办法把这个拉回来，我们得设法把利差压下去。你在这边真正看到的——容我小小地炫耀一下——是一两年、三四年前我上这档播客时，那帮 MMT（现代货币理论）的人正在大喊大叫，说什么债务无关紧要。

turns.en: Acruement saying debt doesn't matter. And I told them I was on a bunch of horses, you know what. Tea rested on the idea that you could issue all the money you want.
turns.zh: 他们一个劲儿地说债务无关紧要。我告诉他们——我当时押了一堆马，你知道吗——MMT 建立在这个理念上：你可以想发多少钱就发多少钱。

turns.en: But when inflation started to actually happen, the government would go and raise taxes or lower spending as a way to go and put the brakes on.
turns.zh: 但当通胀真的开始发生时，政府就会去加税或减支，以此作为踩刹车的办法。

turns.en: And my comment was good luck in prison with that. You're not going to have a politician. They don't have the ability to go get reelected and bring this together when it counts. That was the problem with MMT in a nutshell.
turns.zh: 我的评论是：祝你好运吧，那等于痴人说梦。你不可能指望一个政客——他们没有那种能力，在关键时刻一边还要谋求连任、一边把这事收拾好。这就是 MMT 问题的症结所在。

turns.en: Is it relied upon working against human nature of getting reelected to office? OK, let's pretend we do have a few civilized people that want to go and slowly bring this together.
turns.zh: 它就是依赖于“违背政客谋求连任这一人性”去运作。好，那我们就假想，确实有那么几个讲文明的人，愿意慢慢把这摊事收拾好。

turns.en: We don't have to solve the deficit tomorrow. What we have to do is say we have a path we're committed to to get there. And so what I think is going to happen, these are my predictions.
turns.zh: 我们不必明天就解决赤字问题。我们必须做的，是表明我们有一条自己承诺要去走的路径。所以我觉得接下来会发生的是——这些是我的预测。

turns.en: We're going to uncap... It was on page 15. Uncapital security. So right now it's capped at 184,000. They're going to uncap that. They're going to raise the retirement age slowly.
turns.zh: 我们会取消上限……是在第 15 页。取消社会保障（Social Security）的上限。所以现在它封顶在 184,000 美元，他们会取消这个上限，还会慢慢提高退休年龄。

turns.en: I mean, remember, 65 retirement was from 1936. The equivalent lifespan to what it was in 1936 would be 84 years old now. Can you imagine working to 84 before your Social Security?
turns.zh: 我是说，记住，65 岁退休是 1936 年定的。与 1936 年时相当的预期寿命，放到现在会是 84 岁。你能想象要一直工作到 84 岁才领社会保障吗？

turns.en: That's what it was like back then. They're going to raise the retirement age. You're going to means test Social Security and Medicare. Yes, it was advertised as a trust fund, a lock box.
turns.zh: 当年就是那个样子。他们会提高退休年龄，还会对社会保障和 Medicare（联邦医疗保险）做经济状况调查（means test）。是的，它当初被宣传成一个信托基金、一个上锁的保险箱。

turns.en: You're you're paying for the future. No, it's never been that it was advertised as that. It's always been a straight up tax pays you go and the money is used.
turns.zh: 说什么“你是在为未来缴费”。不，它从来就不是那样，只是被宣传成那样罢了。它一直就是一种现收现付、随收随用的税，钱收上来就被花掉了。

turns.en: Everything else just accounting to make people feel good about it. Where it's going to say Social Security, Medicare, just another tax you're paying.
turns.zh: 其他一切都只是为了让人感觉良好而做的账务处理。将来它会直说：社会保障、Medicare，不过就是你缴的另一笔税。

turns.en: And if you have too high an income or too high an asset, you don't get it. That's fine. Step up basis, get rid of that. The estate tax, there's no reason to be allowing people to go and hide gains.
turns.zh: 如果你的收入太高或资产太多，你就领不到。这没问题。还有“税基递升”（step-up basis），把它取消掉。遗产税方面，没有理由允许人们去藏匿收益。

turns.en: They could defer the gains. I'm good with that, but the gains should be taxed like everything else. So step up basis solves that problem. Some version of Simpson bulls has got to be brought back.
turns.zh: 他们可以递延收益，这我认可，但这些收益应该像其他一切一样被征税。所以取消税基递升就能解决这个问题。某种版本的 Simpson-Bowles（辛普森-鲍尔斯方案）必须被重新搬出来。

turns.en: I'm not sure what I think the bigger thing is if we can get the government to start passing the 70 30 issues. So an issue where the general public is 70 percent in favor of it.
turns.zh: 我不太确定，但我觉得更大的事情是：如果能让政府开始通过那些“70/30”的议题——也就是普通民众有 70% 赞成的议题。

turns.en: If we could start solving those problems, it'll give people the confidence that, yes, we've kind of come back from insanity. And we're going to start to work towards big ideas and implementing policies where most of the country are in favor.
turns.zh: 如果我们能开始解决那些问题，就会让人们有信心：是的，我们已经从疯狂里走回来了，我们要开始朝着那些大理念努力、去落实全国大多数人都支持的政策。

turns.en: I think it's a signal that, yes, we can work together and do things despite the fact that our politics are a little harsh right now. Harley, let's hit page 16 ETFs.
turns.zh: 我觉得这是一个信号：是的，尽管眼下我们的政治有点严苛，我们还是能一起合作、把事情做成。——Harley，我们看第 16 页，ETF。

turns.en: So I've been involved in ETFs for a while now. I just want to highlight quickly just things to watch out for. There's now more ETFs than there are stocks, and it's going to keep on going for plenty of reasons I'm not going to talk about now.
turns.zh: 我涉足 ETF 已经有一阵子了。我只想快速点出几个需要当心的地方。现在 ETF 的数量已经比股票还多，而且出于很多我现在不打算讲的原因，它还会继续增长。

turns.en: Just things to be careful of when you're when you're investing in these things. Number one, leverage. Leverage is not bad. It's a useful tool if used properly.
turns.zh: 就是你在投资这些东西时要小心的一些点。第一，杠杆。杠杆不是坏东西，用得当的话它是有用的工具。

turns.en: The thing to be careful about is it linear or is it the daily percentage? Linear is fine. You go and you buy futures inside an ETF and it levers you up two to one.
turns.zh: 要小心的是：它是线性的，还是按每日百分比的？线性的没问题。你在一只 ETF 里买期货，它给你 2 比 1 的杠杆。

turns.en: That's OK. You make 10% up. You make money going down. It's a linear process. It's a buy and hold strategy. That's good. These daily percentage change ETFs, I would say they're bad, but they're not good.
turns.zh: 这没问题。涨 10% 你赚，跌的时候你亏，它是一个线性过程，是买入并持有的策略，这很好。而这些按每日百分比变动的 ETF，我会说它们不算坏，但确实不好。

turns.en: If you use them for a day or a week, that's fine, man. After that, they're really problematic and the math is very simple. You buy an asset at 100.
turns.zh: 如果你只用一天或一周，那没问题，老兄。但再往后，它们就真的很成问题了，而且这里面的数学很简单。你以 100 买入一项资产。

turns.en: It goes up by 20%. It goes to 120. It goes down by 20%. That's now $24. You're at 96. You go and run the market up and down, up and down. That's called volatility drag.
turns.zh: 它涨 20%，到 120。再跌 20%，也就是跌 24，你就到了 96。你让市场这样上上下下、反复折腾，这就叫波动率拖累（volatility drag）。

turns.en: It will eventually burn that ETF to zero. Next, return of capital. Offering a high yield is eye candy. People just can't help themselves. They want that high coupon.
turns.zh: 它最终会把那只 ETF 烧到归零。接下来，资本返还（return of capital）。提供高收益率就是“眼睛的糖果”，人们就是忍不住，他们想要那个高票息。

turns.en: They feel good about it. What you need to look at is am I getting is the underlying assets in the ETF, generating the income, enough income to cover the distribution, or are they over-distributing?
turns.zh: 他们对此感觉良好。你需要看的是：ETF 里的底层资产所产生的收入，够不够覆盖分红，还是说它们在超额分红？

turns.en: If they over-distribute, that means you're getting some of your money back. And how you'll notice that is when the ETF keeps going down in price month after month without a whole lot changing because they're giving you your money back.
turns.zh: 如果它们超额分红，那就意味着你拿回的是自己的一部分本金。你会发现这一点的迹象是：这只 ETF 的价格一个月又一个月地往下走，而底层其实没怎么变，因为它们在把你的钱还给你。

turns.en: It's a self-liquidating trade. And I would say that probably I won't say most, but many ETFs that are giving you 10% or more are probably having some return of capital involved because to earn more than 10% when junk bonds yield six, seven, eight, it's kind of tough.
turns.zh: 这是一笔“自我清算”的交易。我会说，那些给你 10% 或更高收益的 ETF，很可能（我不敢说大多数，但很多）都涉及某种程度的资本返还，因为在垃圾债收益率只有 6%、7%、8% 的时候，要赚到 10% 以上是相当难的。

turns.en: Finally, we are creating ETFs with more interesting assets in them. Derivatives, total return swaps, things like that. These aren't bad. They're OK, but you need to look at the underlying liquidity of the ETF because what happens is this, these aren't an open-end fund where you get out whenever you want at NAV.
turns.zh: 最后，我们正在创造一些装着更“有意思”资产的 ETF：衍生品、总收益互换（total return swaps）之类的东西。这些不是坏东西，还可以，但你需要看这只 ETF 的底层流动性，因为情况是这样的：它们不是那种你可以随时按净值（NAV）退出的开放式基金。

turns.en: They're not closed-end fund where the assets are totally fixed. They're kind of a hybrid in between. And what happens is the market makers have the ability to buy or sell the ETF at the closing NAV.
turns.zh: 它们也不是那种资产完全固定的封闭式基金，而是介于两者之间的某种混合体。情况是，做市商有能力按收盘净值买卖这只 ETF。

turns.en: What happens is if someone comes in and wants to sell and they have to liquidate some of the ETF, if that asset is sold under the NAV, then the ETF manager will give this person NAV back and not where the manager sold it at.
turns.zh: 会发生的是，如果有人进来想卖、他们不得不清算一部分 ETF，如果那项资产是以低于净值的价格卖掉的，那么 ETF 管理人仍会按净值把钱还给这个人，而不是按管理人实际卖出的价格。

turns.en: And that will harm the fund. We've had a very low volatility, slow rise in equities, relatively slow rise, slow increase in rates, the VIX is what, 17.
turns.zh: 这会损害基金。我们一直处在很低的波动率里，股市缓慢上涨，利率也涨得相对慢，VIX 是多少来着，17。

turns.en: The realized VIX is actually like 10 or 11. The move realized is about 68. So it's not that much. But if we ever get a really volatile market and people want to get in or out of these ETFs, that could be a real problem.
turns.zh: 已实现波动率（realized VIX）其实只有 10 或 11 左右。MOVE 的已实现波动率大约是 68。所以并不高。但如果我们真遇上一个波动极大的市场，而人们又想进出这些 ETF，那可能会是个真正的问题。

turns.en: This is all discussed in a commentary I wrote on my website called Looking Under the Hood of ETFs. I just want to touch on it right now to wet your appetite.
turns.zh: 这些我都在我网站上写的一篇评论里讨论过了，叫《Looking Under the Hood of ETFs》（掀开 ETF 的引擎盖）。我现在只想点一下，吊吊你们的胃口。

turns.en: I go into much more detail there. I urge you to go and look at this thing so you can really understand how ETFs work. They're great products.
turns.zh: 我在那篇文章里讲得详细得多。我强烈建议你去看一看，这样你才能真正理解 ETF 是怎么运作的。它们是很棒的产品。

turns.en: I'm a big fan of them. Just full disclosure, just know what you're getting into. You understand the risk you're taking. So that's that. Harley, final question.
turns.zh: 我是它们的忠实粉丝。只是充分披露一下，你得知道自己踏进的是什么、明白自己承担的风险。就这些。——Harley，最后一个问题。

turns.en: We've had several guests, particularly Michael Evry on this program, tell us that stablecoin statecraft is going to be a really big thing. And specifically what Michael is saying is that we're going to see Secretary Besant continue to push this idea of taking US dollar linked stablecoins.
turns.zh: 我们请过几位嘉宾，尤其是 Michael Evry，在这个节目上告诉我们，稳定币治国术（stablecoin statecraft）将会是一件非常大的事。具体来说，Michael 讲的是，我们会看到 Besant 财长继续推动这个想法——把与美元挂钩的稳定币……

turns.en: And really promoting them as a way of reinforcing the world's commitment to the US dollar is the world's reserve currency. Seems like a good idea on the surface.
turns.zh: 真正地去推广它们，以此强化全世界对“美元是世界储备货币”这一承诺。表面上看像是个好主意。

turns.en: But I also note that it's a setup because once you're on stablecoins, if the world wants to transition away from the US dollar, it becomes a much easier trade and you could abandon US dollars much more quickly in favor of some other stablecoin that's in some other currency.
turns.zh: 但我也注意到，这是个铺垫，因为一旦你用上稳定币，如果世界想从美元转移出去，这就变成了一笔容易得多的交易，你可以更快地抛弃美元，转而用某种以其他货币计价的稳定币。

turns.en: So what do you think about this idea of stablecoin statecraft as policy? Is it something that we should care about? Just to make the big comment here, I do think that Bitcoin at some point is going to zero.
turns.zh: 那么你怎么看“稳定币治国术”这个政策理念？这是我们该关心的东西吗？——先说个大判断：我确实认为比特币（Bitcoin）在某个时点会归零。

turns.en: It's an act of war against a sovereign state. And by the way, Bitcoin can do what 750,000 trades a day. Visa does that much every minute. So Bitcoin as a transactional tool is kind of worthless.
turns.zh: 它是对一个主权国家的战争行为。顺便说一句，比特币一天大概能做 75 万笔交易，而 Visa 每分钟就能做这么多。所以作为一种交易工具，比特币基本上没什么价值。

turns.en: Now, what you're describing is using using a USD stablecoin. I think it's a grand idea because it will be a demand for treasury securities, which is a good thing considering that the Japanese have been selling recently.
turns.zh: 而你所描述的，是使用美元稳定币。我觉得这是个很棒的主意，因为它会带来对国债的需求，考虑到日本人最近一直在抛售，这是件好事。

turns.en: So I'm in favor of that. This notion that it's going to create a path to somebody else. I don't buy that. I don't buy it because the underlying asset, the Russian ruble, the North Korean, whatever they use there, is just not liquid enough to handle the flow of money.
turns.zh: 所以我赞成这个。至于那种“它会为别人另辟一条路”的说法，我不信。我不信是因为其底层资产——俄罗斯卢布、朝鲜用什么也好——根本没有足够的流动性来承接这些资金流。

turns.en: You have to be able to have a liquid instrument. The underlying asset needs to be as liquid as a stablecoin. So I just don't see how they're going to go and create something else to go beat it.
turns.zh: 你必须得有一个有流动性的工具。底层资产需要像稳定币一样有流动性。所以我就是看不出他们要怎么去造出别的东西来打败它。

turns.en: So I think it's a good idea. And by the way, we already have a stablecoin kind of sort of, it's called Denmo. So we're not splitting the atom here to go to a government backed stablecoin.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得这是个好主意。顺便说一句，我们其实已经算是有了一种稳定币，它就叫 Denmo。所以，要转向一个政府背书的稳定币，我们并不是在做什么开天辟地的难事。

turns.en: I think it's a fine idea and I'm not worried at all. Well, Harley, I can't thank you enough as always for a fantastic interview. But before I let you go, tell our listeners what they can expect to find at convexitymaven.com, your website and how to follow your work.
turns.zh: 我觉得这是个好主意，我一点都不担心。——好，Harley，一如既往，我万分感谢你带来这么精彩的访谈。但在我放你走之前，告诉我们的听众，他们能在你的网站 convexitymaven.com 上看到什么，以及怎么关注你的研究。

turns.en: Thank you, Eric. I publish episodically when I have something to say that I think it's interesting. It's free. You can find my entire inventory of my commentaries within my 20 years at convexitymaven.com.
turns.zh: 谢谢你，Eric。我是不定期发表，当我有自认为有意思的东西要说时就写。都是免费的。你能在 convexitymaven.com 上找到我这 20 年来所有的评论文章。

turns.en: I have my podcast there and my other clever ideas. It's free to send me an email. It's on the website and I'll add you to it. They're trying times, Eric, but I will tell you, I'm not going to quite give up yet.
turns.zh: 我的播客、还有其他一些聪明的想法也在那上面。给我发封邮件是免费的，邮箱就在网站上，我会把你加进订阅名单。这是艰难的时代，Eric，但我告诉你，我还不会轻易放弃。

turns.en: We may have problems here, but the U.S. is still the best place out there compared to everything else. So I'll steal Bill Gross's cleanest dirty shirt.
turns.zh: 我们这里也许有问题，但和其他所有地方相比，美国仍然是最好的地方。所以我要借用 Bill Gross 那句话——“最干净的那件脏衬衫”（cleanest dirty shirt）。

turns.en: Well, Harley, you've obviously given us a tremendous amount to think about. And of course, that means it's time now to switch to our market desk segment.
turns.zh: 好，Harley，你显然给了我们大量值得思考的东西。当然，这也意味着现在该切换到我们的市场台（market desk）环节了。

turns.en: Patrick, where's the trade? Thanks, Eric. Now, coming out of Harley Bassman's interview, the trade of the week doesn't have to be another bet on whether yields are going higher or lower.
turns.zh: Patrick，本周的交易机会在哪？——谢谢，Eric。承接 Harley Bassman 的访谈，本周交易（trade of the week）不一定非得是再去押注收益率是涨还是跌。

turns.en: Harley has concerns about fiscal credibility, less fed guidance and mortgage convexity, which points towards potentially more volatile bond markets.
turns.zh: Harley 担心财政公信力、美联储指引减少以及抵押贷款凸性，这些都指向债券市场可能更加波动。

turns.en: So this week I want to own uncertainty through long volatility rather than pick the direction. So I'm looking at the iShares 20 plus year U.S.
turns.zh: 所以本周我想通过做多波动率（long volatility）来“持有不确定性”，而不是去选方向。我看的是 iShares 20 年以上美国

turns.en: Treasury bond ETF ticker TLT trading around $81.27 at the time of recording. Now, January implied volatility has rebounded from about the 10% level to roughly 12%, but it's still at the bottom end of a one year range.
turns.zh: 国债 ETF，代码 TLT，在录制时报价约 81.27 美元。1 月的隐含波动率（implied volatility）已经从大约 10% 的水平反弹到约 12%，但仍处于一年区间的低端。

turns.en: My view is that the uncertainty Harley describes could justify further repricing. The structure is a January 15th, 2027 long strangle, giving us about 120 days.
turns.zh: 我的看法是，Harley 所描述的那种不确定性，足以支撑进一步的重新定价。这个结构是一个 2027 年 1 月 15 日到期的做多宽跨式（long strangle），给我们大约 120 天。

turns.en: In plain English, you are buying a call above the market and a put below it, positioning for a substantial move in either direction, ideally accompanied by a meaningful rise in bond volatility.
turns.zh: 用大白话说，你买一个高于市价的看涨期权和一个低于市价的看跌期权，为任一方向的大幅波动布局，理想情况下还伴随债券波动率的显著上升。

turns.en: I'm looking at the $85 call for around 82 cents and the $77 put for around 97 cents. Those strikes are roughly 5% away on either side and combined costs about $1.79 or about $179 per strangle before fees.
turns.zh: 我看的是 85 美元的看涨，约 82 美分；77 美元的看跌，约 97 美分。这两个行权价大致在市价上下各 5% 的位置，合计成本约 1.79 美元，也就是每份宽跨式约 179 美元（未含费用）。

turns.en: That's just over 2% of the equivalent underlying notional. So we're sacrificing some near spot gamma versus the at the money straddle to reduce the premium outlay while retaining the positive Vega and two sided convexity.
turns.zh: 这大约是等值底层名义金额的 2% 出头。所以，相比平值跨式（at-the-money straddle），我们牺牲了一些近现价的 gamma，以减少权利金支出，同时保留正的 Vega 和双向凸性。

turns.en: Now, January gives the thesis time to develop with potential gains from a strong move either way or a rise in implied volatility before expiration.
turns.zh: 选 1 月，是给这个论点留出展开的时间，有望从任一方向的剧烈波动、或到期前隐含波动率的上升中获利。

turns.en: The tradeoff is that time decay works against us. If held to expiration, we would need roughly a 7% move either way to break even. And if the TLT remains range bound, the entire premium is at risk of loss.
turns.zh: 代价是时间衰减（time decay）对我们不利。如果持有到期，我们需要大约任一方向 7% 的波动才能打平。而如果 TLT 一直区间震荡，整笔权利金都有亏损的风险。

turns.en: So this is a defined premium risk, positive Vega and two sided convexity without needing to call the next directional move in yields. That's where's the trade.
turns.zh: 所以这是一个权利金风险有限、正 Vega、双向凸性的交易，同时又不需要去判断收益率下一步的方向。这就是本周的交易机会。

turns.en: Patrick analyzes and trades the markets every day over at Big Picture Trading. Macrovoices listeners can sign up for a free two week trial at bigpicturetrading.com.
turns.zh: Patrick 每天都在 Big Picture Trading 分析并交易实时市场。MacroVoices 的听众可以在 bigpicturetrading.com 注册，免费试用两周。

turns.en: Now back to Patrick and Maseel. I love the setup pad, especially with where yields are sitting right now. But you know what, let's just keep talking about that because just yesterday, the Federal Reserve delivered this week's defining event raising rates for the first time since 2023, while also signaling that additional tightening may still be required.
turns.zh: 现在把时间交回给 Patrick 和 Maseel。——我很喜欢这个布局，尤其是在当前收益率所处的位置。但你知道吗，我们就接着聊这个，因为就在昨天，美联储交出了本周的决定性事件：自 2023 年以来首次加息，同时还暗示可能仍需进一步收紧。

turns.en: Now, when you put those two things together, you know, oil is staying above 100 and the 10 year treasury yield breaking above 5%. How are you looking at the broader macros?
turns.zh: 把这两件事放在一起看，你知道，油价维持在 100 上方，10 年期国债收益率突破 5%。你怎么看更宏观的大局？

turns.en: We head into the September monthly option expiration tomorrow. All right. Well, let's break this down and let's just start focusing on what happened with the Fed.
turns.zh: 明天我们就进入 9 月的月度期权到期。好，那我们来拆解一下，先聚焦美联储这边发生了什么。

turns.en: Now, we did get the rate hike that was being priced in and it was a hawkish hike as the tone was very clear that there were going to be potentially another rate hike. Now, this actually didn't surprise stir traders.
turns.zh: 我们确实等到了那个已被计入价格的加息，而且是一次鹰派加息，因为基调非常明确：可能还会再加一次。不过，这其实并没有让 STIR（短期利率）交易员感到意外。

turns.en: When you really look at Fed funds futures and the SOFR futures, they were already pricing this in and the reaction to the press conference didn't really move the needle in any way.
turns.zh: 你真去看联邦基金期货（Fed funds futures）和 SOFR 期货，它们早就把这计入价格了，而且对新闻发布会的反应其实没有在任何方面激起波澜。

turns.en: So this was really a lot of commentators talking about it, but really what would happen was Jackson Hole came. We got a very hawkish tilt to Warsh's comments and the market spent the last two weeks doing a substantial repricing in the rates markets and it's been pretty much bond carnage until then.
turns.zh: 所以这其实是一大堆评论员在议论，但真正发生的是：Jackson Hole 会议来了，Warsh 的表态非常鹰派，市场在过去两周里对利率市场做了大幅重新定价，在那之前基本上就是一场债券大屠杀。

turns.en: But really when we heard from Warsh, it really is to me showing that the market priced it right and we're not seeing at least any major reactions to this.
turns.zh: 但真正当我们听到 Warsh 的表态时，在我看来这表明市场定价是对的，至少我们没有看到对此有什么大的反应。

turns.en: So this really to me, like you were suggesting, is really now going to be a story about what happens from here on oil and subsequently the impact that we'll have on treasury bonds.
turns.zh: 所以对我来说，正如你所暗示的，接下来真正的故事，将是油价从这里往后会怎么走，以及随后它对国债的影响。

turns.en: All right, Noah, well, let's take a moment to talk about how the Fed has time the front end of the curve because we're still seeing the 10-year treasury yield hovering at that critical 5% level.
turns.zh: 好，Noah，我们花点时间聊聊美联储是如何把握曲线前端时机的，因为我们仍看到 10 年期国债收益率在那个关键的 5% 水平附近徘徊。

turns.en: In your opinion, does that tell us monetary policy is beginning to work or is that telling us that the market does not believe that the Fed has inflation under control? What do you think?
turns.zh: 在你看来，这告诉我们货币政策开始起作用了，还是告诉我们市场并不相信美联储已经控制住通胀？你怎么想？

turns.en: Well, listen, that 10-year did test 5% and the credibility of the Fed is still a concern that is not resolved. What's interesting is about bond positioning.
turns.zh: 嗯，听着，那个 10 年期确实测试了 5%，而美联储的公信力仍是一个尚未解决的隐忧。有意思的地方在于债券的持仓布局。

turns.en: The interesting part is when we look at those commitment of trader reports on caughtsignal.com, what we see here is that large spec traders continue to aggressively position themselves long, the two and the five year at the front of the curve and staying decisively short, the long end of the curve, clearly positioning for what would potentially be a bull steepener.
turns.zh: 有意思的是，当我们看 cotsignal.com 上的交易者持仓报告（Commitment of Traders）时，我们看到的是：大型投机交易商继续在曲线前端激进地做多 2 年和 5 年，同时坚决做空曲线长端，显然是在为可能出现的“牛市变陡”（bull steepener）布局。

turns.en: This has not yet been rewarding this positioning as we clearly are seeing the entire curve moving at this stage. This is inflation coming in, oil pressing higher, driving that inflation and simply higher rates right across the curve coming in.
turns.zh: 到目前为止，这种布局还没得到回报，因为我们清楚地看到整条曲线此刻都在上移。这是通胀来袭、油价走高推动通胀，进而整条曲线的利率都简单地被推高。

turns.en: What would be interesting to see is that with such a hawkish positioning being priced in on the short end, does this start alleviating pressure on the long end of the curve, which obviously is looking at much longer inflation targets and when you have a Fed that is hawkish and tightening, inevitably it does alleviate pressure on the long end of this curve.
turns.zh: 值得关注的有意思之处是：短端已经计入了如此鹰派的布局，这会不会开始缓解曲线长端的压力？长端显然盯着更长期的通胀预期，而当有一个鹰派、正在收紧的美联储时，它不可避免地会缓解曲线长端的压力。

turns.en: Right now there's a lot of shorts out there betting on that against that 30 year treasury and they have been rewarded as the trend really has been decisively down, but like we heard from Harley, there is room for bond volatility.
turns.zh: 眼下有大量空头在押注、做空那只 30 年期国债，而且他们得到了回报，因为趋势确实是一路坚决向下；但正如我们从 Harley 那里听到的，债券波动率是有空间的。

turns.en: The question is, is it going to play out as everyone's been predicting here? Well, interestingly, when we look at the equities, initially we saw the stock market welcome that Fed decision, but that reaction quickly reversed as the Fed chair there emphasized that inflation remained too high, right?
turns.zh: 问题是，它会像大家一直预测的那样演绎吗？——有意思的是，当我们看股市时，起初我们看到股市欢迎那个美联储决定，但那个反应很快反转，因为美联储主席在会上强调通胀仍然过高，对吧？

turns.en: So we could see a lot more rate hikes going into the future. But with the S&P now approaching negative gamma territory and CTA cell trigger sitting below the market, are we looking at the beginning of a more serious breakdown or can the bulls actually stabilize things and potentially even turn things around?
turns.zh: 所以未来我们可能会看到更多加息。但随着标普现在逼近负 gamma 区域、CTA 的卖出触发点就位于市场下方，我们看到的是一个更严重跌破的开始，还是多头其实能稳住局面、甚至可能扭转形势？你怎么看？

turns.en: What do you think? Well, in the equity markets, it really is a two-sided coin. At this stage, you have the fundamentals still strong. You have resilient earnings, solid economic growth, but on the other side, there are stress points coming from these yields.
turns.zh: 嗯，在股票市场，这真是一枚两面的硬币。现阶段，你的基本面依然强劲：有韧性的盈利、扎实的经济增长；但另一方面，也有来自这些收益率的压力点。

turns.en: The hurdle rate continues to compress multiples and it continues to be a drag on these markets. Now, the fact is that the markets have obviously now been pulling back and we're now battling along a 50-day moving average at a stage where there are some substantial cell triggers sitting right below these markets.
turns.zh: 门槛收益率（hurdle rate）持续压缩估值倍数，也持续对这些市场构成拖累。事实是，市场显然已经在回落，我们现在正沿着 50 日均线拉锯，而在这个阶段，一些相当大的卖出触发点就位于这些市场的正下方。

turns.en: Now, we've already seen things like the Russell small cap indices have a CTA flip, but these trend following systematic trading strategies have cell triggers that are sitting right below these levels.
turns.zh: 我们已经看到，像 Russell 小盘指数这样的品种出现了 CTA 翻转，而这些趋势跟踪（trend following）的系统化交易策略，其卖出触发点就位于这些水平的正下方。

turns.en: Now, the market has not fallen off the edge of the clip. We haven't seen these triggers hit yet. And so it's one of these things that, well, we could have a bullish reversal here in these markets and things can stay stable, but really the bulls have to hold the line right here and now.
turns.zh: 市场还没有跌下悬崖。我们还没看到这些触发点被击中。所以这就是那种情况：我们有可能在这些市场里出现看涨反转、局势稳住，但多头必须就在此时此刻守住防线。

turns.en: We are this morning at the time of recording seeing a little bit of an elevated market on the S&P 500. It'll be very interesting to see whether the market takes a relief from all the stress that it's been in under the last two weeks.
turns.zh: 在录制时的今天早盘，我们看到标普 500 略有走高。市场能否从过去两周所处的种种压力中缓一口气，会非常值得关注。

turns.en: Nonetheless, a lot of cell triggers come in at under 7,500. But I think the base case still should be that the market may be far more rangebound going into the expiration and into the start of next week.
turns.zh: 尽管如此，很多卖出触发点都在 7,500 下方。但我认为基准情形仍应是：在走向期权到期以及下周初的过程中，市场可能会更加区间震荡。

turns.en: All right. Now, let's turn to oil. The other thing moving markets these days because just so many things have been happening, but just in the past 24 hours, we actually saw crude pulling back after Saudi Arabia found additional capacity to move crude through Oman.
turns.zh: 好。现在我们转向原油。这是近来搅动市场的另一样东西，因为发生的事情实在太多了——就在过去 24 小时里，我们实际看到原油回落，因为沙特阿拉伯找到了额外的产能，可以经由阿曼（Oman）输送原油。

turns.en: But even with that news, Brent and WTI both remain above $100. And the underlying supply situation still looks very fragile. Now, when we look at the commitment of traders report, it shows that speculative positioning remains relatively light despite this enormous rally.
turns.zh: 但即便有这个消息，Brent 和 WTI 仍都在 100 美元上方，而底层供应形势看起来依然非常脆弱。当我们看交易者持仓报告时，它显示：尽管有这轮巨大的涨势，投机持仓仍然相对偏轻。

turns.en: So in your opinion, how much of this move is still a short squeezers? How much does it reflect genuine physical market stress? To me, this is where all of the attention is.
turns.zh: 那么在你看来，这轮行情中有多少仍是空头挤压（short squeeze）的成分？又有多少反映了真实的现货市场压力？——对我来说，这正是所有注意力所在的地方。

turns.en: We basically have the physical disruption being very real. The war continues and the Strait of Hormuz traffic continues to be constrained. And we are seeing different arguments that there are some relief coming in.
turns.zh: 我们基本上面临的是非常真实的现货供应中断。战争仍在继续，霍尔木兹海峡（Strait of Hormuz）的通行持续受限。我们也看到各种说法，认为会有一些缓解到来。
